Intake estimates based on food additive levels in the draft General Standard for Food Additives being developed by the Codex Committee on Food Additives and Contaminants, integrated with national data on food consumption, exceeded the ADI of 0-0.7 mg/kg bw for mean intake for the three Member States that submitted such data. In national data submitted by four Member States, estimates of mean intake of TBHQ did not exceed the ADI. The potential exists for consumers of high levels of TBHQ to exceed the ADI, but the available data were insufficient to estimate the number of such consumers or the magnitude and duration of intake above the ADI..

WHO_NSS_GUIDELINE_2023#Pregnancy.title: WHO guideline: Use of non-sugar sweeteners (2023) - recommendation, remarks and pregnant-women evidence
WHO_NSS_GUIDELINE_2023#Pregnancy.scope: Conditional recommendation against NSS for weight control/NCD risk, relevant for everyone including pregnant and lactating women (not people with diabetes); pregnancy evidence limited: preterm birth OR 1.25 (95% CI 1.07-1.46, low certainty), no association with gestational diabetes; polyols are not NSS.

CODEX_CAC_GL_23_1997#Table_Sugars.title: Codex Guidelines for Use of Nutrition and Health Claims CAC/GL 23-1997 (adopted 1997, amended through 2013)

WHO_NSS_GUIDELINE_2023#Children.title: WHO guideline: Use of non-sugar sweeteners (2023) - recommendation, remarks and evidence for children
WHO_NSS_GUIDELINE_2023#Children.scope: Conditional recommendation against NSS for weight control/NCD risk, relevant for children as for adults (not people with diabetes); direct child evidence is limited (one RCT: reduced body fatness, no BMI z-score effect when pooled; observational studies: no significant association; overall certainty low); the guideline does not replace existing safe-intake guidance; polyols are not NSS.

EFSA_CAFFEINE_2015#Children.title: EFSA NDA Panel (2015) Scientific Opinion on the safety of caffeine. EFSA Journal 2015;13(5):4102
EFSA_CAFFEINE_2015#Children.scope: For children and adolescents the available information is insufficient to derive a safe caffeine intake; the adult acute no-concern level (3 mg/kg bw) may serve as a basis for these subgroups; main dietary sources are coffee, tea, caffeinated soft drinks (incl. energy drinks) and chocolate.
